title: Score moteur simplifié (SMS)
short_title: Score moteur simplifié (Simplified Motor Score, SMS)
formula: Addition des points sélectionnés ; points attribués ci-dessous :

how_to_use.why:
The Simplified Motor Score allows providers to rapidly assess trauma patients using a score that is significantly simpler than the GCS, has higher inter-rater reliability and comparable sensitivity for significant traumatic brain injury, the need for neurosurgery and/or intubation and death.

Though the composite GCS has been almost universally adopted, there are concerns about its poor reproducibility and the validity of using the composite score. The SMS offers a convenient and viable alternative.
how_to_use.when: Pour l’évaluation des patients en contexte préhospitalier et de soins aigus pour un éventuel traumatisme craniocérébral.
how_to_use.pearls:
The Simplified Motor Score (SMS) has been suggested as a replacement for the [GCS](nabda:calc.glasgow-coma-scale-score-gcs) in the evaluation of patients for traumatic brain injury.

- A meta-analysis of 5 studies (102,132 total subjects) found that for predicting clinically significant TBI, need for neurosurgery, and need for intubation, the SMS and [GCS](nabda:calc.glasgow-coma-scale-score-gcs) were statistically equivalent.
- A prospective study involving 126 trauma patients found that the SMS had significantly greater inter-rater reliability (83%) than the [GCS](nabda:calc.glasgow-coma-scale-score-gcs) (32%) when performed within 5 minutes of each by two ED physicians who were blinded to the other’s assessments.

**Points to keep in mind:**

- It should be noted that all comparisons of the discriminatory value of the SMS compared to the [GCS](nabda:calc.glasgow-coma-scale-score-gcs) were retrospective reviews of prospectively collected registry data.
- There is no published data on whether observed differences in performance between the SMS and [GCS](nabda:calc.glasgow-coma-scale-score-gcs) are truly clinically insignificant as is asserted by the authors of several of the comparative studies.

next_steps.advice:
The Simplifed Motor Score (SMS) is defined as:

- Obeys commands = 2
- Localizes to pain = 1
- Withdrawals to pain or worse = 0.

Patients with a SMS of <2 are at significantly increased risk of having a significant traumatic brain injury and prompt evaluation and head CT imaging is indicated for these patients.
next_steps.critical_actions: Comme pour le [GCS](nabda:calc.glasgow-coma-scale-score-gcs), les décisions de prise en charge doivent être fondées sur le tableau clinique global du patient. Toutefois, le SMS semble avoir une sensibilité similaire à celle du GCS pour prédire les patients à risque de TBI significatif.
next_steps.management: Les décisions de prise en charge clinique ne doivent pas être fondées uniquement sur le score SMS, bien que des scores <2 soient associés à un pronostic clinique plus défavorable. Le seuil pour réaliser une TDM cérébrale chez ces patients doit être bas.

evidence:
- The SMS was initially validated in a retrospective analysis of 8,347 patients in a prospectively maintained trauma registry of a US Level I trauma center that found it comparable to GCS for its ability to predict the need for ED intubation, neurosurgical intervention, traumatic brain injury and mortality. ([Gill 2005](https://www.pubmed.gov/15635308/))
- A secondary analysis of 21,170 patients from a large prospective trauma database found that the SMS also performed comparably to the total GCS with respect to the same 4 key outcome measures (need for ED intubation, neurosurgical intervention, traumatic brain injury and mortality) with a median difference of 5%. ([Haukoos 2006](https://www.pubmed.gov/17113193/))
- A similar analysis of 19,408 patients in the out-of-hospital setting found the SMS had nearly equivalent discriminatory ability (small statistical differences, but no clinically significant [a priori defined as <5% absolute difference in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve]) compared to the GCS. ([Thompson 2011](https://www.pubmed.gov/21803448/))
- A large retrospective analysis of a statewide trauma registry of 52,412 again found the SMS had comparable sensitivity compared to the GCS for mortality (72.2% vs. 74.6%), traumatic brain injury (40.8 vs 45.4%), need for neurosurgery (52.9% vs. 60%) and intubation (72.7% vs. 75.5%) and conclude the performance of the two score to be “clinically indistinguishable.” ([Caterino 2011](https://www.pubmed.gov/21795294/))
- According a large meta-analysis the SMS was 86-88% sensitive for predicting mortality vs. the GCS which was 90-91% sensitive. Given the large sample size this difference was found to be statistically significant (p = 0.01), though the authors found “the difference to be very small and the clinical significance remained undetermined.” ([Singh 2012](https://www.pubmed.gov/23252405/))
